summary: CAA DNS records let domain owners say which certification authorities may issue certificates for them. RFC 8659 covers certificates for domain names. This document defines a property tag that authorizes CAs to issue S/MIME certificates, with the emailProtection key purpose and rfc822Name address names.

eli5.summary: A domain can post a list of approved ID makers on its door. This adds a line saying which makers may produce email identity cards.

questions: what is the caa issuemail tag
how does caa work for email certificates
what happens if issuemail is malformed
subtitle: A DNS record tag that lets a domain say which certificate authorities may issue email certificates for it.

tldr.problem: RFC 8659 lets a domain restrict which Certification Authorities (CAs) issue certificates for domain names, but it has no way to restrict certificates that certify email addresses.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines the CAA 'issuemail' Property Tag. Its value names the CAs allowed to issue certificates for email addresses at the domain, using the same syntax as the 'issue' tag.
tldr.outcome: A CA must check the domain's 'issuemail' records before issuing an email certificate and must not issue if none of them names the CA. The check supplements normal validation of the email address and does not replace it.

today: RFC 9495 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 8659, which defines the core CAA record.

sections.title: Why Email Needs Its Own Tag
sections.content:
The Certification Authority Authorization (CAA) DNS resource record lets a domain list the Certification Authorities that are allowed to issue certificates for it. RFC 8659 holds the core CAA specification, but its Property Tags restrict only certificates that certify domain names. It does not define a way to restrict certificates that certify email addresses.

For this document, a certificate certifies an email address if it has the id-kp-emailProtection key purpose in the extendedKeyUsage extension and at least one rfc822Name value, or otherName value of type id-on-SmtpUTF8Mailbox, that includes the domain name in the subjectAltName extension.

The new tag is called issuemail. Its syntax and processing are similar to the issue tag from RFC 8659.
sections.eli5: A domain already had a list of who may make website ID cards. Nobody could say who may make email ID cards, so this adds a second list for that.

sections.title: Syntax of the issuemail Tag
sections.content:
One or more issuemail Properties in the Relevant Resource Record Set (RRSet) tell Certification Authorities that the domain wants issuance of email-address certificates restricted.

The value is an optional issuer domain name followed by optional parameters, given in ABNF. The sub-syntax is identical to that of the issue and issuewild tags.

  • issuer-domain-name: the CA's domain name, made of one or more labels.
  • label: ASCII letters, digits and hyphens only (an LDH label).
  • parameters: a semicolon-separated list of tag and value pairs, joined by an equals sign.
sections.eli5: The value is the name of the approved ID maker, maybe followed by extra notes. The rules for writing it are the same as the ones for the website list.

sections.title: How a CA Processes the Tag
sections.content:
Before issuing a certificate that certifies an email address, the CA MUST look for a Relevant RRSet using the discovery algorithm in Section 3 of RFC 8659. The input domain is the domain part of the email address. If that domain is an Internationalized Domain Name with U-Labels, they MUST be converted to A-Labels first.

If the RRSet is empty or has no issuemail Property, the domain has set no restriction. Other tags such as issue or issuewild do not restrict email certificates.

Otherwise the CA compares its own issuer domain name with each issuemail value. If none matches, the CA MUST NOT issue. A value that does not follow the ABNF is treated as if its issuer domain name were the empty string. If the certificate covers more than one email address, the check is done for each one.

Parameters are up to each CA. The RFC defines none and sets no rules for when a CA must act on them. Its example is an account identifier that the CA checks against the requesting account.
sections.eli5: Before making an email ID card, the maker checks the domain's list. If the maker's name is not on it, the maker must say no. A list written in nonsense counts as a list with nobody on it.

sections.title: Worked Examples
sections.content:
The RFC gives five RRSets, all assuming the CA's issuer domain name is authority.example.

  • Only issue records and no issuemail: no restriction on email certificates.
  • A single issuemail ";": the issuer name is empty, so issuance is prohibited.
  • A single issuemail with authority.example; account=123456: the CA may issue or refuse, depending on how it handles the account parameter.
  • One empty record plus one naming authority.example: issuance is permitted, because at least one record matches.
  • A malformed value such as %%%%%: treated like the empty string, so issuance is prohibited.
sections.eli5: If the list is missing, anyone may. If it says nobody, nobody may. If your name is on it anywhere, you may, and if it is gibberish, nobody may.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The considerations in RFC 8659 apply. The issuemail check is a supplement to the CA's validation. A CA MUST NOT treat the presence of its name in an issuemail record as enough proof of the email address, and MUST still validate the address under its policy documents and practice statements.

CAA Properties may carry the critical flag. A CA that does not understand a critical Property MUST NOT issue the certificate. When one RRSet serves several certificate types, a CA's lack of support for a critical Property blocks it from issuing anything for that domain. In the RFC's example, a critical issue record for other-authority.example sits beside an issuemail record for authority.example. If authority.example does not recognize the issue tag, it cannot issue S/MIME certificates for client.example.
sections.eli5: Being on the list is not enough. The ID maker still has to check that the person really owns the email address. And if the list has a must-understand note the maker cannot read, the maker has to stop.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: IANA registered one entry in the Certification Authority Restriction Properties subregistry of the Public Key Infrastructure using X.509 (PKIX) Parameters registry group. The tag is issuemail, its meaning is 'Authorization Entry by Email Address', and the reference is RFC 9495.
sections.eli5: The new tag name was written into the official list of names so nobody else uses it for something different.
